title: NETRA analysis payload
description: The frozen contract between the engine, the workstation, the printed reports and the exports. Validation happens on the payload AS SERVED: the JSON this schema is applied to is the one the API handed out and the one the report was rendered from, so a screen cannot show a shape the contract does not describe. Adding a required field here is a breaking change and requires a SCHEMA_VERSION bump in netra/config.py -- the version travels inside every payload and is printed on every report.

meta.description: Provenance of this payload. Every field here is printed on the reports, because an output that cannot say which engine, which contract and which capture produced it cannot be compared with another output.

window.description: Which batch this payload is about. `id` 0 is the union of every batch, cached under a key rather than a window number: no batch is numbered zero.

fleet.description: The capture's coverage, as read. Present so a page can state 'x of y groups examined' without recomputing it.

entities.description: Wallet groups and network endpoints, ranked by the model's probability. `kind` distinguishes them; only wallet groups are ever ranked as leads. A lead is not a finding of guilt.

id.description: Content-derived identity. NTR-#### for wallet groups, IP-#### for endpoints; the digit count grows only when a new entity would collide with an existing one. An assigned id never changes, and never means anything about the entity itself.

kind.description: wallet is a wallet group; mixer and exchange are wallet groups the structural detectors recognised, kept as their own kind so the map can colour them; ip is a network endpoint, which is never a lead and is never scored.

risk.description: The priority score: the calibrated probability x 100. It ranks groups. It is not a verdict, and it is not the anomaly score -- the two are published separately and never mixed. For an endpoint it is the PEAK risk of the groups it controlled, because an endpoint is not scored itself.

lead.description: Whether this group is raised for review. Always false for an endpoint: infrastructure is context, not a suspect.

confidence.description: The model's own probability for this group, unrounded. It breaks ties in the queue; the anomaly score never does.

typology.description: Named laundering signatures detected at the shipped thresholds. An empty list means none was present at its threshold, which is a statement about the data, not a clearance.

facts.description: Endpoints only: the three numbers the node panel shows instead of a score breakdown, because an endpoint has no score of its own.

explanation.description: Why this score. The listed contributions, the stated remainder and the base must add up to the prediction exactly -- that reconciliation is what makes the number checkable rather than asserted.

features.description: The factors behind the score, largest contribution first.

reasons.description: Findings in plain words, including the exculpatory ones at `info` severity. A tool that only ever shows incriminating factors is not trustworthy.

then.description: An endpoint: context for the map, never a scored group. It has no confidence and no typology because the model never scored it.

edges.description: The picture the map draws. `kind` separates a movement of value (flow) from control of a wallet group by a network endpoint (control): they are different evidence and are never summed. A control edge therefore carries a value ONLY when value actually moved -- an IP address does not transfer bitcoin, and a contract that demanded a number for it would be asking the engine to invent one.

events.description: What changed between batches. Each event shows what changed, from what, to what.

traces.description: Where a lead's money went. Bitcoin is fungible, so a multi-hop trail is a proportional allocation, not an observation -- and the payload says so in `method`.

campaigns.description: Coordinated activity: one attacker cluster, many victims. These are the findings that are not visible wallet by wallet, and the only ones the tool can act on to protect someone. Each entry is an address-poisoning campaign; a pool sweep is published as per-entity features (`sweep_score`, `sweep_ratio`) and as a typology on the sweeping group, because a sweep is a shape one wallet has rather than a group of victims to notify.

cluster.description: The attacker's wallet group, as a NETRA id. The addresses in `addresses` are forged copies; the cluster is the real thing that controls them.

victims.description: Wallet groups that received a lookalike payment.

dust_total.description: Total value sent. Deliberately worthless: the attack is not the money, it is the address that ends up in a transaction history.

addresses.description: The forged addresses themselves, truncated to match what a wallet's display shows.

mimicked.description: The genuine counterparty the forgery copies -- the address the victim has actually transacted with.

lookalike.description: The forged address. Same first four and last four characters as `mimicked`, which is exactly what a truncated display shows.

series.description: The charts' data, published rather than computed in the browser so the screen and the printed report draw the same numbers.

geo_breakdown.description: Share of FLAGGED activity by country, descending. Computed from the flagged set only: the question this answers is where the suspicious traffic sits, not where all traffic sits.

metrics.description: The model's measured performance, on planted ground truth, with the qualifications that belong with it. Read honestly: a linear model over the same features reaches a comparable score, so most of the signal is in the feature engineering.

corpus.description: What ordinary looks like in this capture, so a flagged group's numbers can be read against it.

drift.description: Whether this capture still resembles the training distribution. A drift finding reports; it never rewrites a score.

provenance.description: Who asked for this payload, when, and from which session. Added by the API on the way out, and printed on every report.
